summary: This standards-track document describes how OSPF can gracefully take a link out of service. Raising the metric on one side is not enough to divert traffic flowing in the other direction. The mechanism lets routers on both ends of the link divert traffic before it is shut down.

plainLanguage.summary: Before a link is taken out for maintenance, the traffic on it should be moved somewhere else. This document adds a signal that lets one router tell the router at the other end, and any controller, that the link is about to close, so both sides move their traffic away.

questions: how to gracefully shut down an ospf link
why is raising the ospf metric not enough
what is the ospf graceful link shutdown sub-tlv
subtitle: How an OSPF router warns both ends of a link, and any controller, that the link is about to go down for maintenance.

tldr.problem: Taking a link out of service needs the traffic on it to move away first, but raising the metric on one side only diverts traffic flowing in the other direction.
tldr.mechanism: A router advertises a Graceful-Link-Shutdown sub-TLV on the link. The router at the other end recognises it, raises its own metric for that link to MaxLinkMetric, and both directions of traffic move elsewhere.
tldr.outcome: Maintenance needs one change on one router rather than a change on every router at every end. RFC 8379 is a Proposed Standard that was later updated by RFC 10041.

today: RFC 8379 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2018. It was later updated by RFC 10041, which changed how unreachable links are advertised in OSPF, and it has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why a Link Needs a Shutdown Signal
sections.content:
The document describes a mechanism for taking a link out of service gracefully while still allowing it to be used if no other path is available, and it provides a way to divert the traffic from both directions of the link.

Many OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 deployments run on overlay networks provisioned with pseudowires or Layer 2 circuits. Before devices in the underlying network go offline for maintenance, it is useful to divert traffic away from the node first. The nodes of the underlying network are not visible to OSPF, so the existing stub-router mechanism of RFC 6987 cannot be used. In a service provider's network there may be many customer-edge to customer-edge connections running over a single provider-edge router, and changing the metric on every one of them in both directions is cumbersome.

The mechanism replaces that work with a single change that raises the metric on the remote side as well, and that allows the link to be used as a last resort if no alternate path exists.

The objectives are four. The protocol must advertise the impending maintenance so that traffic from both directions can be diverted away from the link. It must be backward compatible, so that nodes that do not understand the new advertisement do not cause routing loops. It must advertise the maintenance to other nodes so that label-switched-path ingress routers or controllers can learn about it and apply specific policies to reroute the paths in deployments that use traffic engineering. And it must allow the link to be used as a last-resort link, so that traffic is not disrupted when no alternate path is available.
sections.plainLanguage: Raising the cost of a link on one router only moves the traffic that starts on that side. The traffic heading the other way still uses it. This document makes the far-end router react as well, so one change moves traffic in both directions.

sections.title: Where the Information Goes
sections.content:
The graceful-link-shutdown information is flooded in an area-scoped Extended Link Opaque LSA for OSPFv2, as defined in RFC 7684, and in an E-Router-LSA for OSPFv3, as defined in RFC 8362. The Graceful-Link-Shutdown sub-TLV MAY be processed by the head-end nodes or by a controller. The information is advertised as a property of the link and flooded through the area, where it can be used by ingress routers or controllers to take special action.

The mechanism is carried in the flexible encodings of the OSPFv2 Prefix/Link Attribute Advertisement and, for OSPFv3, the E-Router-LSA. Throughout the document, OSPF on its own means the text applies to both versions, and OSPFv2 or OSPFv3 is used where the text is specific to one.
sections.plainLanguage: The signal travels inside link-state advertisements that OSPF already floods across the area, so no new protocol is needed. Every router in the area learns which link is going down.

sections.title: The New Sub-TLVs and TLVs
sections.content:
The OSPFv2 Graceful-Link-Shutdown sub-TLV identifies the link as being gracefully shut down. It is advertised in the Extended Link TLV of the Extended Link Opaque LSA, and has Type 7 and Length 0, so it carries no value of its own.

The Remote IPv4 Address sub-TLV gives the IPv4 address of the remote endpoint on the link. It has Type 8 and Length 4. It is optional and may be advertised in an area-scoped Extended Link Opaque LSA to identify the link when there are multiple parallel links between two nodes.

The Local/Remote Interface ID sub-TLV gives the local and remote interface IDs. It has Type 9 and Length 8, holding 4 octets of the Local Interface ID followed by 4 octets of the Remote Interface ID. It is optional and may be advertised to identify the link when there are multiple parallel unnumbered links between two nodes. The local interface ID is generally readily available, and one mechanism for obtaining the remote interface ID is described in RFC 4203.

The OSPFv3 Graceful-Link-Shutdown sub-TLV is carried in the Router-Link TLV of the E-Router-LSA and has Type 8 and Length 0. The Router-Link TLV already contains the neighbor interface ID, so it can identify the link on the remote node on its own.

The BGP-LS Graceful-Link-Shutdown TLV carries the same information to external entities over BGP, using the format described in Section 3.1 of RFC 7752. It has Type 1121 and Length 0, with no value field, and travels in the BGP Link Network Layer Reachability Information.

Parallel links. Two routers connected by two parallel point-to-point interfaces cannot be told apart by the link information alone: the Extended Link Opaque LSA describes a link by its Link Type, Link ID and Link Data, and the Link Data is the local interface address. A third node, such as a controller or a head-end router, cannot work out which interface on the far router is connected to this particular interface, and might pick the wrong one. Where that matters, a Remote IPv4 Address sub-TLV should be originated and added to the Extended Link TLV. OSPFv3 does not need it, because the Router-Link TLV contains an interface ID and a neighbor's interface ID that together identify the interface on the remote side.
sections.plainLanguage: The shutdown marker itself is an empty sub-TLV. Two more optional sub-TLVs name the link exactly, so that a controller watching several parallel links between the same routers knows which one is meant.

sections.title: What Each Router Does
sections.content:
Every link on a node has its own Extended Link Opaque LSA. The node that has the link to be taken out of service MUST advertise the Graceful-Link-Shutdown sub-TLV in the Extended Link TLV of the Extended Link Opaque LSA for OSPFv2, and in the Router-Link TLV of the E-Router-LSA for OSPFv3, to say that the link is undergoing maintenance. Changing the metric requires the OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 Router-LSAs to be reoriginated, and changing the traffic engineering metric requires the TE Opaque LSAs in OSPFv2 and the Intra-area-TE-LSAs in OSPFv3 to be reoriginated.

When the link is ready to carry traffic again, the Graceful-Link-Shutdown sub-TLV MUST be removed from the Extended Link TLV or Router-Link TLV and the corresponding LSAs MUST be readvertised. The metric MUST be set back to its original value and the corresponding LSAs MUST be readvertised as well.

The exact action taken by the node at the far end depends on the link type.

  • Point-to-point links. The node with the link to be shut down MUST set the metric to MaxLinkMetric, 0xffff, and reoriginate its Router-LSA. The traffic engineering metric SHOULD be set to 0xffffffff and the corresponding TE Link Opaque LSAs SHOULD be reoriginated. When the remote node receives the sub-TLV for a point-to-point link, it MUST identify the local link that corresponds to it, set its metric to MaxLinkMetric, and reoriginate its Router-LSA. It should do the same for the traffic engineering metric. The Extended Link Opaque LSAs and the Extended Link TLV are not scoped for multi-topology, so in a multi-topology deployment the sub-TLV applies to every topology that includes the link, and the receiver should change the metric in the reverse direction for all of them. When the originator purges the Extended Link Opaque LSA or reoriginates it without the sub-TLV, the remote node must reoriginate the appropriate LSAs with the original metric values.
  • Broadcast and NBMA links. These networks are represented by a star topology with the Designated Router at the centre, so routers advertise only their adjacency to the Designated Router and do not form adjacencies with each other. The MaxLinkMetric on the remote link cannot be changed, because all the neighbours are on the same link and setting the cost to MaxLinkMetric would affect every path through any of them. The node with the link to be shut down MUST set the metric to MaxLinkMetric and reoriginate its Router-LSA, and should set the traffic engineering metric to 0xffffffff and reoriginate the TE Link Opaque LSAs. For a broadcast link the two-part metric of RFC 8042 is used, and the node originating the sub-TLV MUST set the metric in the Network-to-Router Metric sub-TLV to MaxLinkMetric and reoriginate the corresponding LSAs. The nodes receiving the two-part metric should follow the procedures in that RFC, including its backward-compatibility procedures to keep the routing loop-free.
  • Point-to-multipoint links. Operation is similar to point-to-point. The remote node MUST identify the neighbour that corresponds to the link, set its metric to MaxLinkMetric, and reoriginate its Router-LSA with the changed metric for that neighbour.
  • Unnumbered interfaces. These have no unique IP address and borrow one from another interface. A similar procedure to the one in RFC 2328 is applied, with the Link Data field of the Extended Link TLV holding the Local Interface ID instead of an IP address. The Local/Remote Interface ID sub-TLV MUST be advertised when there are multiple parallel unnumbered interfaces between two nodes.
  • Hybrid broadcast and point-to-multipoint interfaces. Operation is similar to the point-to-multipoint case. When the sub-TLV is received for a hybrid link, every remote node connected to the originator MUST set its metric for that neighbour to MaxLinkMetric and reoriginate its Router-LSA.
sections.plainLanguage: The router with the link raises its cost to the maximum and says so. The router at the far end sees the message and raises its cost for the same link, so traffic that was heading towards the link turns around as well. On a shared network the rule is different, because raising the cost there would affect every other router on it.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility
sections.content: The mechanisms are fully backward compatible. It is required that the node advertising the Graceful-Link-Shutdown sub-TLV, and the node at the remote end of the link, both support the extensions described in the document for the traffic to be diverted. If the remote node does not support the capability it will still use the graceful-shutdown link, and there are no other adverse effects. For broadcast links using two-part metrics, the backward-compatibility procedures of RFC 8042 apply.
sections.plainLanguage: An older router that does not understand the signal simply keeps using the link, and nothing breaks. Both ends have to support the mechanism for the traffic to actually move.

sections.title: Where This Is Used
sections.content:
Overlay networks. A service provider offers Layer 2 services to a customer whose own interior gateway protocol joins the customer's sites into one private network across the provider's network. When a provider-edge router goes out for maintenance, the provider sets it to stub-router state and communicates the pending work to the customer's networks. Changing the metric on every corresponding Layer 2 circuit in both directions is tedious and error-prone, so the customer router sets the graceful-link-shutdown state on its links to the other customer sites, changes the metric to MaxLinkMetric and reoriginates the corresponding LSA. The far end of each of those links does the same, and traffic in both directions moves away from the router being maintained. The link stays usable as a last resort, so traffic is not disrupted when no alternate path exists.

Controller-based deployments. Where the controller takes part in the interior gateway protocol, it can also receive the graceful-link-shutdown information as a warning that maintenance is imminent, and use it to find alternate paths and to reroute label-switched paths away from the affected link. If no alternate path satisfies the constraints, the controller may relax them temporarily and put the service on a different path. Raising the link metric on its own is not enough as a signal, because the metric can also rise for other reasons such as LDP to IGP synchronisation.

Layer 3 VPN services and sham links. When a provider-edge router goes out of service, all the links on it can be set to graceful-link-shutdown state, which guarantees that traffic to and from dual-homed customer routers is diverted. The same applies to sham links, where traffic can be diverted from both ends without touching the configuration on the remote side of the sham links.

Hub and spoke deployments. OSPF is largely deployed with many spokes connecting to one or more hubs for redundancy. The stub-router mechanism can divert spoke-to-spoke traffic away from an overloaded hub, but traffic flowing from the spokes through the hub into an external network may not be diverted in some cases. When a hub goes down for maintenance, all its links can be set to graceful-link-shutdown state, and traffic is diverted from the spoke sites as well without configuration changes on the spokes.
sections.plainLanguage: The document gives four situations where this saves work: a provider router in the middle of many customer connections, a controller planning traffic engineering paths, a virtual private network router going down, and a hub router in a hub-and-spoke design. In each case one change on the affected router diverts the traffic.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document uses the OSPF packets and LSAs described in RFC 2328, RFC 3630, RFC 5329 and RFC 5340. The authentication procedures for OSPFv2 in RFC 2328 and for OSPFv3 in RFC 4552 apply to this document as well. It introduces no further security issues beyond those discussed in RFC 2328 and RFC 5340.
sections.plainLanguage: The signal travels in the same OSPF packets as everything else, so the existing OSPF authentication rules cover it and no new security rules are needed.
